records.label: F1
records.segregation: Phenotype not linked to the 1p21.1-q23.3 locus
quotes: We herein describe a new multigeneration family with 11 affected individuals (F1), in whom we confirm intra-familial clinical variability. Facial asymmetry, a clinical feature not highlighted in other ACS reports, was highly prevalent among the patients reported here.
Interestingly, this locus was not linked to the phenotype segregating in F1.

records.label: F1
records.segregation: Duplication segregated with the disease; all unaffected individuals negative (LOD 2.88), suggesting full penetrance
quotes: The Brazilian family (referred to as F1; online supplemental table 1) is a non-consanguineous family with 11 members showing the typical characteristics of ARCND. Of those documented, the majority presented with question mark ears (8 of 10), microstomia (8 of 10) and micrognathia (6 of 10), with considerable intrafamilial variability observed.
The duplication spanned 430 302 bp (NC_000007.14:g.18437239_18867540dup) telomeric to TWIST1, covering most of the HDAC9 gene.

Breakpoint amplification and Sanger sequencing within the family demonstrated segregation of the duplication with the phenotype (figure 1B). All unaffected individuals were negative, suggesting full penetrance in this family

notes.statement: In a four-generation Brazilian family with ARCND, Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022) found no pathogenic variants in PLCB4, GNAI3, or EDN1, and linkage analysis assuming autosomal dominant inheritance gave a maximum LOD score of 2.88 (maximum theoretical 2.93) in a 17.6-Mb region on chromosome 7, narrowed by microsatellite markers to chr7:14395902-28158440 (hg38).
quotes: The highest LOD score (2.88), which is close to the threshold value of ≥3.0 for significance and the maximum theoretical LOD score for this family (2.93), was observed in a region of about 17.6 Mb on chromosome 7 (chr7:14395902–32017194 (hg38); table 1).
Genotyping of microsatellite markers narrowed the chromosome 7 linkage region to chr7:14395902–28158440 (hg38)

notes.statement: Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022) found by targeted resequencing a 430-kb tandem duplication (NC_000007.14:g.18437239_18867540dup) beginning about 280 kb telomeric of TWIST1 and covering most of HDAC9. Several shorter HDAC9 isoforms were duplicated whole, while the full-length catalytically active isoforms were predicted to be disrupted.
quotes: Targeted resequencing of a 2.4 Mb region around TWIST1 revealed no potential pathogenic variants in TWIST1, but did detect a tandem duplication within HDAC9 that was only present within the three affected family members tested

Multiple transcript isoforms of HDAC9 are duplicated in their entirety (including transcript isoforms 3, 8, 9, 10 and 11); however, full-length catalytically active transcript isoforms (transcript isoforms 1, 5, 6 and 7) extend beyond the breakpoint and therefore are likely to be disrupted by this duplication.

notes.statement: Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022) performed Capture-C from the TWIST1 promoter in human embryonic calvarial mesenchymal cells. The most frequent cis interactions were telomeric of TWIST1, within HDAC9 and the duplicated region. This suggested that the region holds TWIST1 regulatory elements, which would give the duplication a possible pathogenic mechanism.
quotes: The highest frequency of interactions was telomeric of TWIST1, particularly within the HDAC9 gene and the region spanned by the duplication (figure 1A). This implies that this region contains regulatory elements involved in the control of TWIST1 expression, providing a possible pathogenic mechanism for the duplication.

notes.statement: Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022) found that neural crest cells derived from patient iPSCs had higher HDAC9 (3.15-fold) and TWIST1 (2.03-fold) expression than controls. Patient cells also migrated less well (4.3-fold decrease). Patient mesenchymal cells had lower alkaline phosphatase activity and less matrix mineralisation during osteogenic differentiation, which the authors took to indicate delayed or impaired osteogenesis.
quotes: However, an increase in HDAC9 (3.15-fold, unpaired t-test p=0.009) and TWIST1 (2.03-fold, unpaired t-test p=0.03) mRNA was observed in the ARCND-iNCC (figure 2A, B) compared with controls (unpaired t-test).
a significant decrease in migratory capacity of ARCND iNCCs was observed compared with controls (4.3-fold decrease, Student’s t-test, p=0.0009)
Together, these results indicate a delay or impairment of osteogenic differentiation.

notes.statement: Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022) found 19 DECIPHER patients with copy-number gains in the region. Seven had ear malformations and 7 had micrograthia, and most of these duplications included the TWIST1 enhancer eTW6. A 179-kb duplication lying wholly inside the ARCND duplication but not including the TWIST1 regulatory elements was found in a patient without ARCND features.
quotes: Analysis of CNVs in DECIPHER (https://decipher.sanger.ac.uk/) revealed 19 patients with copy-number gains in the region.
Interestingly, one of the DECIPHER duplications (276644; 179 kb) is enclosed entirely within the ARCND duplicated region; however, this patient does not have ARCND clinical features

notes.statement: Masotti et al. (2008) ran a genome-wide linkage analysis in 2 large families with auriculocondylar syndrome. They found evidence of linkage to 1p21.1-q23.3 in one family (F2) (maximum lod score 3.01 at theta = 0), and named this locus ACS1. Three loci for other first and second pharyngeal arch disorders had been excluded first.
quotes: Through segregation analysis, we first excluded three known loci associated with disorders of first and second pharyngeal arches (Treacher Collins syndrome, oculo-auriculo-vertebral spectrum, and Townes-Brocks syndrome).
we observed evidence of linkage to 1p21.1-q23.3 in F2 (LOD max 3.01 at theta=0)

notes.statement: Masotti et al. (2008) found that the 1p21.1-q23.3 locus was not linked to auriculocondylar syndrome in a second large family (F1). They concluded that at least 2 loci are responsible for the phenotype.
quotes: Interestingly, this locus was not linked to the phenotype segregating in F1.
showed evidence for genetic heterogeneity, suggesting that there are at least two loci responsible for this phenotype

notes.statement: Masotti et al. (2008) described auriculocondylar syndrome as an autosomal dominant disorder of the first and second pharyngeal arches. Its features are malformed 'question mark' ears, prominent cheeks, microstomia, an abnormal temporomandibular joint, and hypoplasia of the mandibular condyle. Penetrance appeared complete, with high variability within and between families.
quotes: Auriculo-condylar syndrome (ACS), an autosomal dominant disorder of first and second pharyngeal arches, is characterized by malformed ears ('question mark ears'), prominent cheeks, microstomia, abnormal temporomandibular joint, and mandibular condyle hypoplasia.
Penetrance seems to be complete, but there is high inter- and intra-familial phenotypic variation
